claims.claim: Bail is a conditional release mechanism, and the Supreme Court in Stack v. Boyle (1951) described its function as assuring the accused will stand trial and submit to sentence, with the traditional right to freedom before conviction permitting unhampered preparation of a defense and preventing punishment before conviction.

Under Stack v. Boyle, bail set at a figure higher than an amount reasonably calculated to fulfill the purpose of assuring the defendant's presence is excessive under the Eighth Amendment, and bail must be fixed on standards relevant to the individual defendant rather than by inference from the indictment alone.

In United States v. Salerno (1987) the Supreme Court, 6-3 in an opinion by Chief Justice Rehnquist, rejected facial challenges to the pretrial detention provision of the Bail Reform Act of 1984 under both the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause and the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Bail Clause, holding the detention regulatory rather than punitive.

The Excessive Bail Clause has never been held to create a general right to bail; Salerno states that the Clause 'says nothing about whether bail shall be available at all' and quotes Carlson v. Landon for the proposition that the English clause from which it was taken was never thought to accord a right to bail in all cases.

The Supreme Court has said the Eighth Amendment's proscription of excessive bail 'has been assumed to have application to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment,' language that stops short of a holding on incorporation.

18 U.S.C. 3142, added by the Bail Reform Act of 1984 (Pub. L. 98-473, title II, sec. 203(a), Oct. 12, 1984, 98 Stat. 1976), gives a federal judicial officer four options: release on personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond, release on conditions, temporary detention, or detention.

Section 3142(c) requires the least restrictive condition or combination of conditions that will reasonably assure appearance and safety, and section 3142(c)(2) provides that a judicial officer may not impose a financial condition that results in the pretrial detention of the person.

Section 3142(f) requires an adversarial detention hearing with counsel, testimony, proffer, and cross-examination, allows continuances of up to five days for the defendant and three for the government, does not apply the rules of evidence, and requires that a finding that no conditions will reasonably assure safety be supported by clear and convincing evidence.

Section 3142(e) creates rebuttable presumptions that no conditions will suffice - one triggered by a prior qualifying conviction committed while on release and within five years, and one triggered by probable cause to believe the defendant committed specified drug, firearm, terrorism, human-trafficking, or minor-victim offenses.

Federal pretrial services exist in every judicial district other than the District of Columbia, and their statutory functions include collecting and verifying information about the defendant, reporting to the judicial officer before the release hearing with a recommendation on conditions, and supervising people released on conditions.

Commercial bail bonding for profit is rare internationally; the Conference of State Court Administrators' 2012-2013 policy paper states that the United States and the Philippines are the only countries that permit the widespread practice of commercial bail bonds.

A commercial surety typically charges the defendant a non-refundable premium, commonly about ten percent of the bail set by the court, and often requires collateral covering the full bond amount; bond schedules set release amounts by charge without an individualized assessment.

At midyear 2023, local jails in the United States held 664,200 people, of whom 70 percent (467,600) were unconvicted - awaiting court action on a current charge or held for other reasons - and 30 percent (196,600) were convicted; people admitted from July 2022 to June 2023 spent an average of 32 days in custody before release.

The unconvicted jail share cannot be read as a count of people detained because they could not afford bail: BJS counts within it people held for other reasons, and 90,500 jail inmates in 2023 were held for federal, state, or tribal authorities.

Using the release tendencies of quasi-randomly assigned bail judges, Dobbie, Goldin, and Yang (2018) estimated that pretrial detention increases the probability of conviction largely through more guilty pleas, has no net effect on future crime, and reduces formal-sector employment and receipt of employment- and tax-related government benefits.

Pretrial risk assessment instruments are genuinely contested: the Pretrial Justice Institute, formerly a proponent, published a 2020 statement opposing them on grounds of biased input data and weak predictive power, while Desmarais, Monahan, and Austin (2022) argue in Criminal Justice and Behavior that the empirical evidence behind those critiques is lacking.

State bail law varies substantially and is an area of active change: New Jersey moved to a risk-based system effective January 1, 2017 through a voter-approved constitutional amendment and implementing statute, and Illinois abolished the requirement of posting monetary bail, a change the Illinois Supreme Court upheld in Rowe v. Raoul on July 18, 2023 with its stay vacated on September 18, 2023.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether pretrial risk assessment instruments are accurate enough, and fair enough, to inform release decisions
positions: Pretrial Justice Institute (2020): the instruments are built from data produced by biased enforcement, cannot separate willful flight from missed appearances, cannot reliably predict rare violent outcomes (it cites an AUC of 0.644 for one widely used failure-to-appear model against a 0.7 threshold used in other fields), and lend a false appearance of precision; the organization reversed its own earlier support.

Desmarais, Monahan, and Austin (2022, Criminal Justice and Behavior): the empirical basis for those critiques is lacking; rigorous studies find good accuracy in predicting new criminal activity including violent crime, including across racial and ethnic groups, and the instruments can reduce pretrial detention when their results actually inform decisions.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both positions by name and does not adjudicate between them. It notes that the disagreement runs partly on statistics (what counts as adequate discrimination for a rare outcome) and partly on values (whether a group-level probability may justify restricting an individual's liberty before conviction), which is why more data has not ended it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Bail Clause binds the states
positions: Schilb v. Kuebel (1971) says the proscription of excessive bail 'has been assumed to have application to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment.'
That phrasing is an assumption recorded in passing, not a holding, and the Supreme Court has not squarely decided the question the way it decided incorporation of the Excessive Fines Clause.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the Court's own careful wording - that application to the states has been assumed - rather than asserting that the Clause has been incorporated. Every state constitution or code supplies its own bail provisions in any event.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How to read the share of the jail population that is unconvicted
positions: The figure is sometimes presented as a count of people jailed because they cannot afford bail.

BJS defines the unconvicted category as people awaiting court action on a current charge or held in jail for other reasons, and separately reports 90,500 people held for federal, state, or tribal authorities in 2023.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the BJS figure with its date and its own definition, and states explicitly that it is not a measure of unaffordable bail.

rightsIssues: Supreme Court opinions, the Illinois Supreme Court opinion, and the United States Code are edicts of government and are in the public domain; short quotations from the opinions are used and marked as quotations.

The BJS report, the federal judiciary page, the COSCA policy paper, the NCSL page, and both risk assessment sources state no reuse license and are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY; their facts were synthesized and all prose was written for EliExplains.

sourceRecords.title: Stack v. Boyle, 342 U.S. 1 (1951)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (United States Reports, vol. 342, via govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full bound-volume PDF (18 pages) and extracted its text. Verified: No. 400, argued October 18, 1951, decided November 5, 1951; opinion by Chief Justice Vinson; Justice Minton took no part; separate opinion by Justice Jackson joined by Justice Frankfurter. Supports: federal law from the Judiciary Act of 1789 through Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 46(a)(1) provided that a person arrested for a non-capital offense shall be admitted to bail; the traditional right to freedom before conviction permits unhampered preparation of a defense and serves to prevent the infliction of punishment prior to conviction; release before trial is conditioned on adequate assurance that the accused will stand trial and submit to sentence; and the excessiveness standard - 'Bail set at a figure higher than an amount reasonably calculated to fulfill this purpose is "excessive" under the Eighth Amendment.' Also supports that bail must be fixed on standards relevant to the individual defendant, and that the judgment below was vacated and remanded.

sourceRecords.title: United States v. Salerno, 481 U.S. 739 (1987)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (United States Reports, vol. 481, via govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full bound-volume PDF (31 pages) and extracted its text. Verified: No. 86-87, argued January 21, 1987, decided May 26, 1987; opinion by Chief Justice Rehnquist joined by White, Blackmun, Powell, O'Connor, and Scalia; Marshall dissenting joined by Brennan; Stevens dissenting (6-3). Supports: pretrial detention under 18 U.S.C. 3142(e) is regulation rather than punishment because Congress framed it as a response to crimes by persons on release, and the incidents of detention are not excessive in relation to that goal; the Excessive Bail Clause 'says nothing about whether bail shall be available at all'; the Court's quotation of Carlson v. Landon, 342 U.S. 524, 545-546 (1952), that the bail clause was lifted from the English Bill of Rights and has never been thought to accord a right to bail in all cases; the Court's treatment of the Stack language as dictum; the statement that 'when Congress has mandated detention on the basis of a compelling interest other than prevention of flight ... the Eighth Amendment does not require release on bail'; and the closing line that 'In our society liberty is the norm, and detention prior to trial or without trial is the carefully limited exception.' Also supports the clear-and-convincing standard and the enumerated procedural safeguards.

sourceRecords.title: Schilb v. Kuebel, 404 U.S. 357 (1971)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States (United States Reports, vol. 404, via govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full bound-volume PDF and extracted its text. Verified: No. 70-90, argued October 12, 1971, decided December 20, 1971; opinion by Justice Blackmun. Supports two points used in the lesson: the Court's statement that 'the Eighth Amendment's proscription of excessive bail has been assumed to have application to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment' while the case was 'not at all concerned ... with any fundamental right to bail'; and the description of the Illinois ten-percent deposit bail system (personal recognizance, a ten-percent deposit bond with one percent of the bail retained as costs, or a full-amount deposit).

sourceRecords.title: 18 U.S.C. 3142 - Release or detention of a defendant pending trial
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives
sourceRecords.license: U.S. federal statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Primary authority for the federal release-or-detain framework. Page states text current through August 18, 2026. Source credit: added Pub. L. 98-473, title II, sec. 203(a), Oct. 12, 1984, 98 Stat. 1976. Supports: the four dispositions in subsection (a); the subsection (b) default of personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond; the subsection (c) 'least restrictive further condition, or combination of conditions' rule and the enumerated conditions including a bail bond with solvent sureties; the subsection (c)(2) rule that a judicial officer 'may not impose a financial condition that results in the pretrial detention of the person'; subsection (d) temporary detention of up to ten days excluding weekends and holidays; subsection (e) detention after a hearing and the rebuttable presumptions in (e)(2) and (e)(3); subsection (f) hearing timing and the five-day defense / three-day government continuances, the rights at the hearing, the inapplicability of the rules of evidence, and the requirement that a safety finding be supported by clear and convincing evidence; subsection (g) factors; and subsection (i) written findings and separate housing from convicted persons.

sourceRecords.title: Jail Inmates in 2023 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 309965)
sourceRecords.provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry record, reused with the same id and URL. For this lesson I re-read the report PDF at https://bjs.ojp.gov/document/ji23st.pdf (Zhen Zeng, April 2025, NCJ 309965) and extracted its text directly. Supports: 664,200 people held in local jails at midyear 2023; 70 percent (467,600) unconvicted, 'either awaiting court action on a current charge or held in jail for other reasons,' and 30 percent (196,600) convicted; people admitted to local jails from July 2022 to June 2023 spent an average of 32 days in custody before release; and 90,500 jail inmates held for federal, state, or tribal authorities in 2023, which is why the unconvicted share cannot be read as a count of people held on unaffordable bail.

sourceRecords.title: Evidence-Based Pretrial Release (2012-2013 Policy Paper)
sourceRecords.provider: Conference of State Court Administrators (author Arthur W. Pepin; staffed by the National Center for State Courts)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full 19-page PDF text from the copy posted by the Colorado Commission on Criminal and Juvenile Justice; the paper itself is the Conference of State Court Administrators 2012-2013 policy paper and no first-party COSCA URL could be verified as reachable. Supports the money-bail vocabulary (citation release, release on recognizance, conditional release, deposit bond, full cash bond, property bond, surety, commercial bail agent, compensated surety), the description of commercial bonding practice (a non-refundable premium usually about ten percent of the bail set, often with collateral), the use of bond schedules, and the statement that 'The United States and the Philippines are the only countries that permit the widespread practice of commercial bail bonds.' The paper is a policy advocacy document: it recommends presumptive non-financial release and evidence-based risk assessment, and the lesson attributes that recommendation to COSCA rather than stating it as fact.

sourceRecords.title: The Case Against Pretrial Risk Assessment Instruments
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full 12-page PDF text, dated November 2020. Advocacy document, used only as evidence of the position its authors hold. Supports: the Pretrial Justice Institute, a former proponent, released a 2020 statement opposing pretrial risk assessment instruments; its stated grounds are that the tools are built from biased data, cannot reliably distinguish willful flight from missed appearances, cannot reliably predict violence because violence is rare, and add 'a veneer of scientific objectivity and mathematical precision to what are really very weak guesses about the future'; and its accuracy argument that the Public Safety Assessment's failure-to-appear model has an AUC of 0.644 while many disciplines treat below 0.7 as poor discrimination.

sourceRecords.title: The Empirical Case for Pretrial Risk Assessment Instruments
sourceRecords.provider: Criminal Justice and Behavior (SAGE, for the International Association for Correctional and Forensic Psychology)
sourceRecords.notes: Sarah L. Desmarais, John Monahan, and James Austin, Criminal Justice and Behavior 49(6): 807-816 (2022), DOI 10.1177/00938548211041651. The publisher page returned HTTP 403, so the article PDF was read from the copy posted by Multnomah County, Oregon (https://multco.us/file/the_empirical_case_for_pretrial_risk__assessment_instruments_/download) and its text extracted; the DOI is registered as the canonical URL. Supports the opposing scholarly position: the authors respond to three critiques - poor accuracy, racial bias, and increased detention - and argue that rigorous research shows the instruments have good accuracy in predicting new criminal activity including violent crime even across race and ethnicity groups, and can help reduce pretrial detention when their results actually inform decisions. The article notes it draws on an open letter to the Pretrial Justice Institute endorsed by a list of named pretrial risk-assessment scholars.

sourceRecords.title: The Effects of Pretrial Detention on Conviction, Future Crime, and Employment: Evidence from Randomly Assigned Judges
sourceRecords.notes: Will Dobbie, Jacob Goldin, and Crystal S. Yang, American Economic Review 108(2): 201-240 (2018), DOI 10.1257/aer.20161503. Read the publisher's article page and abstract. Supports the attributed research finding that, using the release tendencies of quasi-randomly assigned bail judges as an instrument, pretrial detention increased the probability of conviction largely through more guilty pleas, had no net effect on future crime, and reduced formal-sector employment and receipt of employment- and tax-related government benefits. Cited as one study's estimate, not as settled consensus.

sourceRecords.title: Rowe v. Raoul, 2023 IL 129248
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of Illinois (Illinois Official Reports)
sourceRecords.license: State judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the full 30-page official-reports PDF from the Illinois Courts resource host and extracted its text. Verified: Docket 129248, filed July 18, 2023; Chief Justice Theis delivered the opinion, joined by Justices Neville, Cunningham, and Rochford; Justice O'Brien specially concurred; Justice Overstreet dissented joined by Justice Holder White; circuit court judgment reversed. Supports: Public Acts 101-652 and 102-1104 provide that 'the requirement of posting monetary bail is abolished' and make pretrial release on personal recognizance the default; the Illinois Constitution does not mandate monetary bail as the only means of assuring appearance or protecting the public; the court's order that sixty days after the opinion, on September 18, 2023, its stay of the pretrial release provisions would be vacated; the dissent's contrary reading of the crime victims' rights clause; and the historical note that Illinois effectively eliminated professional bail bondsmen in 1963 by requiring release on a ten-percent deposit.

sourceRecords.title: Criminal Justice Reform
sourceRecords.provider: New Jersey Courts (Administrative Office of the Courts)
sourceRecords.notes: The New Jersey Judiciary's own program page. Supports: New Jersey's reform rests on a voter-approved constitutional amendment implemented by statute effective January 1, 2017; it moved the state from a system relying principally on monetary bail to a risk-based system; the Public Safety Assessment is used to inform release decisions and Pretrial Services officers monitor released defendants; and the law sets deadlines for indictment and disposition for detained defendants. The January 1, 2017 effective date is independently corroborated by the Rowe v. Raoul dissent's citation to Holland v. Rosen, 895 F.3d 272, 279-80 (3d Cir. 2018).

sourceRecords.title: Pretrial Release Toolkit
sourceRecords.notes: Nonpartisan legislative service organization. Page last updated January 29, 2024. Supports only the neutral framing points used: state law provides the framework determining who is eligible for pretrial release and on what conditions, most defendants are eligible for release, and pretrial release has been an area of sustained state legislative activity over the past decade. No policy position taken from this source.
